title: Hands, Eyes, and Ears
objectives: I can tell how things feel with soft, sticky, and bumpy.
I can tell how much sound with loud and quiet.
I can use a describing word to say how something feels or sounds.
rationale: Sensory words let children describe what they touch and hear, and they are some of the first describing words children use in writing. Soft, sticky, and bumpy are about touch; loud and quiet give the first natural opposite pair, which prepares the opposites unit later in the year. The unit also revisits sort and match, because children sort objects by touch, and calm, because quiet and calm often go together in the classroom.

passage.title: Nina and the Touch Box
paras: Nina puts her hand in the touch box. She feels something soft.
Her fingers find something bumpy, and then something sticky. "Yuck!" she says.
The class stays quiet while she guesses. She pulls out a glue jar, and the whole class gets loud with laughter.

qs.q: Nina's fingers find something sticky. What does sticky feel like?
qs.why: Sticky is like glue; the jar she pulls out at the end is a glue jar.

qs.q: Why does the whole class get loud at the end?
qs.why: The story says the class gets loud with laughter.

qs.q: What does Nina feel first in the box?
qs.why: She feels something soft before the bumpy and sticky things.

teacher.overview: Children learn five describing words by touching objects in a feely box and by making sounds, then hear them in a short story. They use the words to say how things feel and sound; everything is oral.

notes.va.soft.adj: Use a feely box with cotton, a stuffed toy, and a rock. Soft here means gentle to touch; children may also use it for a quiet voice, which is a different use, so stay with touch first.
notes.va.loud.adj: Compare a drum tap and a drum bang, and a whisper and a shout. Loud is about how much sound, not how fast. Pair with quiet right away so children hear the contrast.
notes.va.quiet.adj: Practice a quiet signal and a quiet voice. Children may think quiet means no talking at all; it can mean little sound, such as a whisper.
notes.va.sticky.adj: Use tape, glue sticks, and a damp sponge, not food, to avoid allergies. Sticky is about holding on to your fingers; wet and sticky are not the same, so test each object.
notes.va.bumpy.adj: Use sandpaper, an orange peel, and a smooth plate. Bumpy is the opposite of smooth; have children run a finger over each. A bumpy road can also be a bumpy ride, which they may notice.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I put my hand in the box. It is not hard. It feels gentle. It is soft, like a bunny. Now I make a sound with the drum. It is easy to hear. That is loud. When I whisper, it is quiet.'
discuss: What is the softest thing in our room?
Where in school do we use a quiet voice, and why?
extend: Play a feely-bag guessing game where children name the thing and one describing word.
Make a loud and quiet sound chart with pictures, and sort cards to match.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit sort and match by having children sort objects into soft and hard piles and match each to a word. Use quiet again with calm in unit 6 when children stretch and move with a quiet body, and loud again in unit 7 as part of opposites.

frames: A ___ is loud, and a ___ is quiet.
wida.oral: Partner A hides an object in a bag and touches it without looking. Partner B asks, 'Is it soft?' or 'Is it bumpy?' until Partner A says the object.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (suave, fuerte, silencioso, pegajoso, rugoso) have not been reviewed by a native speaker; suave and blando both fit soft, and fuerte also means strong.
Sense boundary: soft is taught as a touch word (gentle to touch); the sense of a quiet voice, as in a soft voice, is left for grade 1.
Sense boundary: bumpy is taught as a texture (covered with small bumps); the ride sense appears in an example but is not separately taught.
Teaching choice: sticky uses glue and tape in the passage and notes, not food, to avoid allergy concerns.
